name: Eyebrow microblading

lead: Microblading fills thin, sparse or uneven brows with fine hair-like strokes of pigment, giving thicker, darker, more defined brows that are visible as soon as the session is done. Men who want stronger brows discuss it for that reason.

A technician draws the strokes with a handheld tool into the upper layer of the dermis, where the pigment stays visible until it fades. Published literature is mostly reviews and case reports of complications, and forum opinions vary on how natural the result looks.

paras: It is done as a salon or clinic session, with the technician choosing a pigment shade and brow shape to match your face. Results last up to about two years, with a touch-up usually suggested around six weeks later and then every 12 to 18 months. People often keep brows trimmed and groomed around the new shape.

Case reports describe granulomatous reactions, sarcoidosis, allergic contact dermatitis, cellulitis and a reported mpox transmission. As with any tattoo, unclean equipment is the main route to infection. Regulation varies by region, and people with pigment allergies or skin conditions around the brows may want to avoid it.

angle.text: Microblading tattoos hair-like pigment strokes into thin or uneven brows, so fuller, darker, more defined brows are visible straight away and last up to about two years. Men weigh how natural the strokes look against the gain in density. Published literature is mostly case reports of side effects.

lead: Microblading is a semi-permanent cosmetic tattooing technique in which a technician uses a handheld tool with fine blades or needles to draw hair-like strokes of pigment into the upper dermis of the eyebrows. It is used to fill sparse, thin or uneven brows and to disguise brow loss.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports results can last up to about two years, with a touch-up recommended around six weeks later and then every 12 to 18 months.[2] Published clinical literature consists largely of reviews and case reports of complications, including granulomatous reactions, sarcoidosis, allergic contact dermatitis, cellulitis and a reported mpox transmission.[3][4][5][6][7][8]
In looksmaxxing forums, microblading is discussed by men who want thicker, darker brows, with opinions that range from favourable to critical of how natural the results look.[9][10]
infobox: About 6 weeks after, then every 12-18 months[2]
Not federally regulated in the US; provincial in Canada[2]

paras: Microblading is described as a form of superficial micropigmentation in which pigment is deposited as far as the papillary dermis with a manual tool, unlike machine tattooing.[1][2] Practitioners map the brow shape, and pigment is typically iron-oxide based, producing dark brown or black shades.[2]

Eyebrow tattooing began as a way to cover medical brow loss and became more common for cosmetic purposes in the 1980s and 1990s in the US and Asia. Microblading, often called eyebrow embroidery, became popular in Singapore by about 2007 and in the US and Canada by the mid-2010s.[2] A 2021 review attributes much of its popularity to social media awareness.[1]

Wikipedia lists misapplied pigment, migration, colour change and hyperpigmentation as common problems, with serious complications uncommon but including bloodborne infection and reactions to pigment ingredients.[2] Case reports document delayed granulomatous reactions,[4][5] cutaneous sarcoidosis,[6] Koebner phenomenon,[3] allergic contact dermatitis in a person with nickel sensitisation,[7] and preseptal cellulitis.[8] A 2023 report described mpox transmission attributed to contaminated equipment.[9] A 2022 review covers technical and clinical complications of cosmetic tattooing generally.[10]
A 2020 pilot study in four patients with skin types III-IV reported successful removal of cosmetic eyebrow tattoos with a picosecond laser and a perfluorodecalin-infused patch.[11]

No controlled trials of the cosmetic effect were identified. The published literature is mainly a 2021 review of the technique and its science,[1] a four-patient laser-removal pilot study,[11] and case reports of complications.[3][4][5][6][7][8][9]

A looksmax.org thread points to looks theorists who regard thick, dark brows as important and asks whether men have tried microblading.[12] Another thread asks about suitability for men with dark hair and light brows; the poster says most before-and-after videos looked unnatural or female-shaped, and replies range from saying the results looked better to saying the look is obviously artificial, with some suggesting minoxidil or peppermint oil instead.[13] Other threads ask whether minoxidil can be continued after microblading.[14]

lore.intro: Forum discussion treats microblading as a harder-end brow option and debates whether it looks natural on men.[12][13]
